question: Austria Power Grid’s plans for a 380 kV overhead power line between East Tyrol and south-east Carinthia

Austria Power Grid (APG) is planning a 380 kV overhead power line spanning approximately 180 km from Lienz (East Tyrol) to Völkermarkt (south-east Carinthia), which is to pass straight through highly sensitive Alpine forest areas. The plan involves pylons up to 90 m high, resting on concrete foundations with an area of 20 x 20 m.

In addition to the health impacts feared by local residents and the impairment to quality of life and housing, there are risks of significant land take, soil compaction, adverse effects on native flora and fauna and their biodiversity, as well as long-term and large-scale deforestation and permanent disfigurement of the natural scenery.
The project is therefore in flagrant contradiction with the objectives of the Alpine Convention and with the requirements of EU law on the protection of forests and the restoration of nature. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the project’s compatibility with the Alpine Convention and the relevant provisions of EU law?

As guardian of the Treaties, what measures does the Commission intend to take to urge the APG to adopt a less harmful approach that protects the landscape and nature, namely the laying of underground or underwater cables?
answer: The EU has not ratified the Alpine Convention protocols on Nature Protection and Landscape Conservatio n (1), and on Mountain Forests (2), which could be relevant for the case, although they apply in Austria. By contrast, the Convention’s Energy Protocol (3) was ratified by the EU in 2006 and forms part of both Austrian and Union law. Its Articles 2, 10 and 12 contain relevant provisions on power lines.

The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive (4) requires an EIA for projects likely to have significant environmental effects, including overhead electricity lines above 220 kV and longer than 15 km (5).

The project, which is currently in the planning phase (6), appears to fall within that scope and therefore requiring an EIA, which must examine all likely environmental effects, including under the Birds Directive (7) and the Habitats Directive (8), (9). On top of the public engagement which is compulsory for projects with a status of a Project of Common Interest, the EIA Directive also ensures public participation.

Member States are therefore primarily responsible for assessing these projects and ensuring their compliance with Union energy and environmental law and the Alpine Convention and its Energy, Nature Protection and Landscape Conservation, and Mountain Forests protocols, also when only in force in the specific Member State. In addition, the Convention has its own compliance mechanism (10).
